items.body: The Canyon County Sheriff’s Office on Friday confirmed its investigation into the Vallivue School District’s 2024 land deal is still active. Idaho EdNews broke the story on April 17. “No updates at this time, investigation still active,” a detective with the criminal investigation division told EdNews Friday. The district in 2024 bought 87 acres of farmland from Dave Christensen, the father of trustee Clay Christensen, for $5 million. The land, intended for the site of a school, was appraised at $2.87 million. “I knew about what I wanted, and, you know, it was really the only way I probably would have sold it,” Dave Christensen told EdNews in April about his $5 million price tag for the land. Idaho code requires trustees to have property appraised before a purchase and that appraisal “shall be used to establish the value of the real property.” Superintendent Lisa Boyd at the time defended the purchase and said the district complied with statute. Later that month, EdNews obtained records from several other Idaho school districts that showed Vallivue’s deal bucked the norm by millions. Five different land purchases in districts from around the state came in under the appraised value — and in two deals landowners gifted chunks of property — according to public records EdNews examined in a spot check of transactions over the past two decades. Vallivue trustees have declined to answer any questions about the land deal. Trustee Toni Brinegar, who was board chair at the time of the 2024 purchase, referred EdNews to their attorney. Two trustees have since resigned, leaving the board with three members. Brinegar resigned in June, and Paul Tierney resigned in August. Boyd said both trustees had planned to resign after their kids graduated from Vallivue schools. The district is looking for interested residents to apply for the vacancies.

Brad Little’s office on Wednesday, April 1, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) An Idaho judge on Thursday ordered a Boise minister who was found guilty of misdemeanor trespass during a political protest to pay $357 in fines — but not serve more jail time. The Rev. Sara LaWall, the minister for the Boise Unitarian Universalist Fellowship, and eight others who were protesting bills restricting transgender rights were arrested this spring after refusing to leave the lobby to the office of Idaho Gov. Brad Little, whom the protestors said they were hoping to meet with. LaWall’s defense attorney cast her actions during the protest as an act of civil disobedience, an act that involves intentionally breaking laws for moral reasons. In a statement before the judge delivered his sentence, LaWall, who has a transgender daughter, said she had repeatedly attempted to relay her concerns over anti-trans bills with elected officials. “We followed every available path of redress (grievenances) within our system. Our fears and concerns, and frankly, our begging and pleading, went unheard and unanswered,” LaWall said, citing legislators cutting off testimony early on an anti-trans bill where doctors planned to testify. She said she understands her actions have consequences, and she said she accepts full responsibility for her actions. “I do not take this lightly,” LaWall said. “I knew the risks when I chose to stay. But I was willing then and am willing now to accept the risks as an act of faithful witness and solidarity with my daughter, all the beautiful trans youth, and the incredible trans community here in Idaho. Many of whom I am blessed to call my friends and chosen family — all of whom must negotiate risk and their own safety every day, just by being who they are.” Before issuing the sentence, Idaho 4th District Judge Adam Kimball said he was weighing several factors — such as protecting society and deterring LaWall and others from violating the law. But he said he didn’t find probation necessary in this case. “It’s my hope that you will be heard the way you wish, and that if you are not, that you do not break the law to be heard. But I don’t find that placing you on probation is necessary to achieve that end,” the judge said. “Your conduct, whatever it may have been, waiting for an appointment, a protest, was peaceful, was considerate,” he added. The judge’s sentence for LaWall was for the state’s recommended minimum $500 in fines, plus $170 in court costs, which the judge tacked on after the case went to a jury trial and one day in jail for which he granted LaWall credit. The judge also granted LaWall credit toward her fees for her $300 cash bail. The Rev. Sara LaWall drops hearts down the rotunda of the Idaho State Capitol Building. Protestors on April 2, 2024, dropped 48,000 handmade hearts — meant to represent LGBTQ Idahoans — in protest of anti-LGBTQ legislation. items.body: The Ada County Courthouse is pictured in this file photo on Sept. 17, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) The Constitution Party candidate in Idaho’s 1st Congressional District election has pleaded guilty to possessing “child sexually exploitative material.” He is still eligible for office under the U.S. Constitution. Brendan Gomez, 27, was arrested in early July by Ada County Sheriff’s Office detectives at a home in Boise, Channel 2 Idaho News reported. He was booked into the Ada County jail and held on $500,000 bail, according to the jail roster. He was charged with 10 counts of willfully possessing child sex abuse material, according to state court records. He entered a plea deal Monday, pleading guilty to two counts of possession of sexually exploitative materials. His sentencing hearing is scheduled for Nov. 16, according to court records. The state recommended Gomez serve a fixed term of three years in prison, with 12 years indeterminate. Gomez’s attorney could not be immediately reached for this story. Gomez also ran for Congress in 2024, earning about 1.5% of the vote in the general election. In 2022, he ran unsuccessfully against incumbent state Sen. Lori Den Hartog to represent District 22 in the Idaho Legislature. Gomez’s name will still appear on the ballot for the Nov. 3 general election. He is running against incumbent Republican U.S. House Rep. Russ Fulcher, Democrat Kaylee Peterson, and independent Sarah Zabel. The deadline to withdraw from the ballot was Sept. 4. Under the Idaho Constitution , convicted felons are ineligible for state or local office until they fulfill their sentence, but there are no such restrictions for federal elected officials. Members of the U.S. House must be at least 25 years old, a U.S. citizen for at least seven years, and an inhabitant of the state they represent.The U.S. Constitution does not otherwise limit eligibility. Under U.S. House rules , members who are convicted of a crime with a sentence of two or more years of imprisonment “should refrain” from participating in votes and “should resign” from any committee. items.body: Boise State University and the University of Idaho have received lackluster grades from a nonprofit group that advocates for campus free speech. But if graded on a curve, the Boise State and U of I grades look a little bit better. Both universities received a “D” from the Philadelphia-based Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression . Using student surveys, FIRE ranked 261 colleges and universities; 121 received failing grades. The September 2025 slaying of conservative activist Charlie Kirk had far-reaching effects, FIRE said. Some colleges denied recognition for chapters of Kirk’s Turning Point USA, while nine schools punished faculty members who publicly criticized Kirk. “The overall state of free speech on campus is grim,” FIRE President and CEO Greg Lukianoff said in a news release. “Too many college administrators wield their power to cancel controversial speakers, cave to government or student calls for censorship, and limit academic freedom.” FIRE rated only two Idaho universities. Click on the links for the full reports on Boise State and the U of I . Here are a few thumbnails. Boise State: overall ranking, 59 of 261 Boise State earned a top 50 ranking for “political tolerance,” a signal that students are willing to host controversial speakers. But the university ranked in the bottom 50 for “openness,” according to the FIRE report, “meaning many contentious topics feel off-limits to students.” Anonymous student quotes from FIRE’s survey One student reported an exchange from class: A professor said she was very upset with the outcome of the presidential election, and asked students to sum up their thoughts in one word. The student had a response in mind, contentment, but was reluctant to express it. “I thought I would get attacked or judged if I said that,” the student wrote. Another student, a lesbian, said she is often frightened to discuss her partner’s gender. “I am afraid of my fellow students.” Boise State student survey results, by the numbers 47% of students say they have self-censored, at least once or twice a month. 70% of students say it’s acceptable, at least in rare cases, to preempt an event by shouting down a speaker; 32% said the use of violence to prevent a speech is acceptable, at least in rare cases. Boise State has roughly 1.03 liberal students for every one conservative student. Boise State response “We appreciate FIRE’s focus on the importance of free expression in higher education,” the university said in a statement. “We will consider the findings, including the student feedback reflected in the survey, as we continue our ongoing work to support a campus culture that encourages open inquiry and the free exchange of ideas.” U of I: overall ranking, 87 of 261 U of I also ranked in the top 50 for “political tolerance.” However, the U of I received a bottom 25 ranking for “self-censorship,” indicating students frequently stay silent. items.body: Here’s a not-so-bold prediction: It won’t take the State Board of Education a tortured 16 months to hire the next University of Idaho president. This next search almost has to go more smoothly than the last presidential search — the one that finally ended on July 1, when David Hahn took the reins at Boise State University . Smooth and transparent are two different things, however. And transparency is a thing of the past, due to a new state law that moves the presidential search process almost entirely out of public view. Retiring University of Idaho President C. Scott Green (U of I photo) " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/C.-Scott-Green-graduation-e1789667075837-1180x765.jpg" class="wp-image-125466 size-large" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/C.-Scott-Green-graduation-1180x787.jpg" alt="" width="1180" height="787" /> Retiring University of Idaho President C. Scott Green (U of I photo) So perhaps sometime next spring or thereabouts, the State Board will announce a successor to U of I President C. Scott Green , who announced his retirement last week. The vast majority of the Vandal family — students, parents, faculty and staff, alums and donors — will have only a vague idea of how the board reached its decision. They’ll never really know why the board made its pick, or who else wanted the job. In other words, expect lots of secrecy. What else can we expect this time around? Here are a few other predictions, based on the Boise State search. Expect a slower start . Actually, that’s happening already. In March 2025, Marlene Tromp put the State Board squarely on the clock. She abruptly accepted the University of Vermont presidency , in the middle of Boise State’s spring semester, with plans to leave at the end of the school year. The State Board announced its presidential search committee the day after Tromp accepted the Vermont job. The goal — perhaps unworkable from Day One — was to find Tromp’s replacement in time for the 2025-26 school year. Because Green is retiring, and not switching jobs, he is giving the State Board a lot longer runway. He will stay on at the U of I through June 30, the end of the academic year. That’s important, because college and university presidents often switch jobs in the summer. The State Board will be in no hurry to get the U of I job on the market for the summer hiring rush. At the front end, that gives the State Board a little more time to assemble a search committee and hire a search firm. It doesn’t mean the search will be more transparent. Just less pell-mell. The search committee could offer a big tipoff . The new law sets minimum requirements for the search committee: two State Board members, two university employees, two alumni, a foundation representative and a community representative. That’s all. (And no, students aren’t guaranteed a seat at the table.) There’s nothing stopping the State Board from naming more committee members. Or stacking an eight-member committee with a distinct emphasis. Regardless, watch the committee makeup. It matters, a lot. David Hahn, the sole finalist for the Boise State presidency, speaks to reporters in a Tuesday, June 16, 2026 press conference. items.body: Teachers and secondary students in the Nampa School District will get new MacBooks next year in a move to counter the rising cost of PCs as AI data companies gobble up the supply of computer parts. Nampa students have been using 11-inch HP Pro laptops that run on Windows, but trustees on Tuesday approved a four-year, $5.6 million lease agreement with Apple to switch to 13-inch MacBook Neos for students in grades 6-12. For years, Apple laptops have been more expensive than PCs. But Assistant Superintendent of Operations Cortney Stauffer told the school board that has changed. He said the switch to Apple will save an estimated $1.4 million over four years. Elementary students will continue to use iPads. Cortney Stauffer, executive director of operations for the Nampa School District " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108-944x1180.jpg" class="wp-image-105832 size-thumbnail" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108-160x200.jpg" alt="" width="160" height="200" srcset="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108-160x200.jpg 160w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108-496x620.jpg 496w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108-944x1180.jpg 944w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108-1229x1536.jpg 1229w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108.jpg 1536w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 160px) 100vw, 160px" /> Nampa Assistant Superintendent of Operations Cortney Stauffer “The PCs, believe it or not, are now significantly more expensive than an Apple Neo,” Stauffer said. Nampa’s switch to Apple comes months after the Boise School District made the same move. Boise trustees in July approved a five-year, $18 million lease agreement with Apple for 22,000 devices. “What we saw coming is a dramatic increase in prices,” Boise Director of People and Organization Services Will Goodman said. As EdNews reported in July , Idaho school districts face soaring PC prices as AI data centers buy up computer parts. Boise’s own Micron Technology, a large producer of computer memory and storage, announced in December that it made the “difficult decision” to exit the consumer market and sell only to AI companies to accommodate the “surge in demand” for data centers. Gordon Howard, director of technology for Bonneville School District, told EdNews that Micron’s exit is leading to higher costs for all sorts of technology. He said the cost of Chromebooks has increased by $100 over the past year, and the cost to buy new servers for the district increased from $6,000 to $10,000 within three months. “It’s not just Chromebooks,” Howard said. “It’s everything.” The resale value of Chromebooks is low compared to Apple products. Bonneville in July sold 1,488 Acer Chromebooks for $5 a piece. Howard said the district usually keeps Chromebooks for seven years, but that model of Acer Chromebooks became too expensive to maintain after just four years. Screens and keyboards were breaking. “It was just going to cost us too much to maintain them,” he said. “The breakthrough rate was just too high.” By switching to MacBooks, Nampa hopes to avoid that issue. The lease agreement includes 6,000 MacBook Neos for students and 650 MacBook Airs for teachers. At the end of the lease, the district will own the devices and can sell them back to Apple with a guaranteed buyback price of $120 for the Neos and $275 for the Airs. “This is actually a wonderful opportunity for the district,” Stauffer told trustees. Currently, students in Nampa are responsible for all damage to the PCs. Repair costs range from $50 to $120. Parents can purchase insurance for $25 a year to avoid those costs. But with the move to Apple, the district will get rid of the laptop insurance program. One of them called to cut a set of programs that help peo
items.body: Members of the Idaho Legislature's Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee and their staff tour Southwest Idaho Treatment Center, or SWITC, in Nampa on Nov. 20, 2024. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun) In January, as Idaho state lawmakers prepared for budget cuts, the state’s governor laid out a list of options for Medicaid decreases. One of them called to cut a set of programs that help people with disabilities live in their homes. In the end, lawmakers only adopted a more narrow cut to disability care. As federal protections fade, Americans with disabilities fear a return to institutions But as Idaho’s tight budget years dwell — and the federal government softens its stance on prioritizing keeping people with disabilities in their homes instead of in institutions — disability advocates are growing worried that home care might face cuts. Expanded decades ago, home and community-based services have become a staple for state Medicaid programs. But as the Trump administration seeks to reinterpret a U.S. Supreme Court decision that serves as a foundation for expanded rights of people with disabilities to receive care in their homes, disability advocates worry that home and community-based services could be threatened. Advocates maintain that the underlying laws requiring home care options remain. The federal government’s stance — detailed in a recent memo by the U.S. Justice Department — comes before states will see the impact of massive federal Medicaid cuts enacted in President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. “When (states’) federal funding shrinks, they’re going to be reluctant to replace it with state funding, and so they will be tempted to try to reduce funding for home community-based services,” retired Idaho disability rights attorney Jim Baugh said. “But, I presume without a plan for what to do with the people who lose those services, or who have their services reduced, because we don’t have any alternative. So I just see this leaving people in the lurch. I see this being a dangerous possibility.” Several advocates also worry that there aren’t enough institutional settings to care for people with disabilities, if home and community-based services faced cuts. items.body: A mother holds hands with her son on a swing set. At least seven states have passed laws making equally shared parenting time the legal default in child custody cases. (Photo by Troy Bennett for Maine Morning Star) A growing number of states are making an equal split between parents the default child custody option in divorce cases. Louisiana and Mississippi this year joined at least five other states that have adopted the so-called 50-50 standard — four of them since 2021, as more legislators rework divorce-related laws that remained mostly unchanged for years. The 50-50 custody issue does not break down cleanly along partisan lines: The Mississippi bill was sponsored by Republicans, the Louisiana legislation by Democrats. Both states’ laws explicitly codify a custody guideline that many courts in other states follow. Supporters say a formal 50-50 custody standard makes divorce proceedings more equitable for fathers — who historically have been awarded less custody time than mothers — and encourages them to maintain an active role in their children’s lives. And it can reduce friction between separating parents by signaling they’re both starting the custody process on an equal playing field, said Don Hubin, board chair of the National Parents Organization, an advocacy group that has pushed for more states to adopt legal presumptions of shared parenting. Without that presumption, Hubin said, one or both parents may feel like they have to paint each other in a bad light in order to ‘win’ more time with their children. “It’s not just about the practice of shared parenting, but about the law signaling to parents that this is going to be the outcome unless something special is going on in your case,” he said. “It reduces the anxiety of the parents, which reduces the conflict between the parents.” But critics say the standard might harm vulnerable women and children by making it more likely that children must spend time with a parent who isn’t safe. They fear that for women in abusive marriages, the knowledge they would have to cede 50% of their child’s time to an unsafe parent could push them to remain in a marriage just to protect their children. Kimberly Rummage, who lives in Kentucky, calls her state’s 50-50 custody standard “absolutely diabolical.” She’s had a lengthy battle in court with her ex-husband over custody of their child. “I think that parents should have to prove why they get that 50-50,” she said. “You should have to show what you’ve done in that child’s life, what you know about that child, how you’ve participated and supported that child.” Some critics also argue that the 50-50 standard doesn’t account for the needs of children at different ages. Mississippi state Rep. Dana McLean, a Republican, warned her colleagues the state’s new law could harm breastfeeding infants who need to spend most of their time with their mothers during their first months of life. Mississippi’s new law requires family courts to use equally-shared parenting time as the default in custody cases. Parents seeking more time must present evidence showing why a 50-50 split isn’t in their child’s best interest. It also changes how child support is calculated: The new formula for 50-50 custody can lower child support payments for the parent with the lower income. Louisiana’s new law says child custody “shall” be divided equally, rather than “should,” which was the language under the previous law. In both states, as in others that have adopted the 50-50 standard, a judge can override the rule if the court finds credible evidence for awarding more time to one parent. But in Mississippi, several judges spoke against the bill before it passed, saying the old system — in which custody was awarded on a case-by-case basis using a specific set of factors — was the most fair. Through the first two months of fiscal year 2027, which began July 1, Idaho’s revenue collections have come in $51.2 million ahead of projections, according to the August edition of the fIscal year 2027 General Fund Budget Monitor. For the month of August, strong individual income tax collections that exceeded the monthly projection by $40.8 million helped push overall revenue collections ahead of forecast. Although it is still very early in the fiscal year, Idaho is projected to end the fiscal year June 30 with a positive ending balance of $657 million if state revenue collections come in as forecasted for the remainder of the fiscal year. Scott Grow, a Republican from Eagle who serves as co-chairman of the Idaho Legislature’s Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee. items.title: Bringing Idaho’s education decisions back where they belong
items.summary: (Boise) – As a state, Idaho is often described as self-reliant and independent. We take pride in local control, including when it comes to our public education system. Unlike some other states, we do not look to Washington D.C. to govern our local communities. We know what we need – and how to get it done. As the U.S. Department of Education continues its work to restore state control and localize
items.body: (Boise) – As a state, Idaho is often described as self-reliant and independent. We take pride in local control, including when it comes to our public education system. Unlike some other states, we do not look to Washington D.C. to govern our local communities. We know what we need – and how to get it done. As the U.S. Department of Education continues its work to restore state control and localize educational governance nationwide, Idaho has put itself at the forefront of making the most of an opportunity to make our public system work for Idaho students – not for students in California or Washington D.C. This is a common-sense acknowledgement that different states and communities have needs that are best understood by the people who live and serve in them. The Idaho Department of Education has recently applied for – and was granted – a federal waiver that will allow the state to make its own decisions on the spending of certain federal dollars. This work was done in response to a general complaint that when states receive federal dollars for education, they have limited authority in how to use those funds to maximize student outcomes. Now, with this federal waiver, schools are better positioned to meet local needs. Idaho is now a proud member of states granted Ed Flex waiver status and is eager to make itself a leader when it comes to state-led improvements in K-12 public education. Simply put: the federal government gives schools a set of rules to follow. An Ed-Flex waiver gives a state permission to change some of those rules if there is a better way to help students learn. There is an additional waiver to be submitted later this month. The Returning Education to the States waiver is designed to provide flexibilities that honor the principle that the people who know their students best – parents, teachers, principals, schools, and states – should have more authority to make decisions that fit their needs. The waiver brings decision making closer to students, reduces unnecessary paperwork, and allows schools to use their federal resources in a way that works for them. These waivers, in addition to reducing state and federal testing for Idaho students, should send a clear message to Idahoans about where we stand when it comes to the importance of small government and local control. Idaho will continue to strengthen its reputation as a state where families feel confident in their public schools, where taxpayers feel assurance that their dollars are being well-handled and well-spent, and where students can work towards a successful future in their own communities and beyond. This is a major victory for Idaho’s kids and further reinforces that in this state, we value prudent, conservative stewardship of taxpayer dollars. The best answers for Idaho’s schools are found around kitchen tables, in local communities, and inside Idaho classrooms. By rolling back federal overreach, protecting parental rights, and honoring local leadership, we can build an education framework that reflects Idaho values, respects local taxpayers, and equips every child in our state to succeed.

items.summary: The University of Idaho could get rid of its last standardized test requirement. items.body: The University of Idaho could get rid of its last standardized test requirement. If the change goes into effect for fall 2027, it would bring the U of I in line with other colleges and universities in the region, a university spokeswoman said Tuesday. The proposed change also comes in the midst of an evolving national debate over standardized tests. Most colleges and universities don’t require ACT or SAT scores, and some don’t look at them at all, but some of the nation’s most selective schools are reinstating testing requirements. For the vast majority of applicants, the U of I is already test-optional . High school graduates with a GPA of 3.0 or higher are admitted automatically, with no test required. The same goes for in-state students who score proficient of higher on the Idaho Standards Achievement Test. Graduates with GPAs of 2.3 to 2.59 don’t need to submit a test score either; they enroll through the Vandal Gateway Program for first-year general studies majors. The test requirement only applies to students that fall in a donut hole — with GPAs of 2.6 to 2.99. About 11% of the U of I’s incoming class falls within this range, spokeswoman Jodi Walker said. The U of I had dropped all testing requirements during the COVID-19 pandemic. Officials began looking at the U of I’s sole testing requirement in the spring, as this year’s application season drew to a close. This year’s numbers suggest the U of I’s recent enrollment surge is slowing — and probably for a number of reasons, including a shrinking population of 18- to 22-year-olds, and a rising public debate over the value of a four-year degree. University officials decided the testing requirement was one easy lever to pull, Walker said. “The landscape is changing,” she said. “Why put up barriers that don’t necessarily need to be there?” The decision, for now, falls to interim Provost Brooke Blevins . If Blevins signs onto the proposal, the admissions change would go into effect on an interim basis, kicking off a two-year faculty review. That would give the faculty time to see if the change is having an impact on enrollment and access, Walker said. Idaho colleges and universities set their own admissions guidelines — and Boise State University, Idaho State University and Lewis-Clark State College do not require SAT and ACT scores. Standardized test mandates have fallen out of favor nationally, and are rare in the West. According to the National Center for Fair & Open Testing (FairTest), a Brooklyn, N.Y.,-based group, only 7% of colleges and universities require standardized tests . The vast majority of colleges fall into a broad category of test-optional schools — and despite the U of I’s limited testing requirement for some students, FairTest lists the U of I as test-optional. According to FairTest, all colleges in Idaho and its neighboring states are test-optional or “test-free,” which means test scores aren’t even considered in the admissions process. But all eight Ivy League colleges and universities are reinstating their pre-COVID standardized testing requirements, and other top-ranking schools are following suit, Higher Ed Dive reported in August . The schools are facing some external pressure from the Trump administration, which favors standardized testing. FairTest Executive Director Harry Feder downplayed the trend. “Ivy Plus schools, as wealthy, exclusive national outliers, have increasingly gone back to requiring test scores for admission for their own institutional reasons and in response to external pressures,” he said in a recent news release. “The national picture of test-optional and test-free admissions is actually very stable.”

items.body: The Boise School District’s enrollment is down 699 students compared to last fall, according to a report presented to the school board Monday. The 3% dip isn’t a surprise. District leaders projected and planned for a 600-student decrease when they set their budget for the current school year. And it continues a trend that started about a decade ago. Since 2015, Boise’s enrollment has dropped 22%, from 28,078 to 21,805 this fall. On Monday, district administrator Jason Hutchison gave trustees two possible reasons for the downward curve: a declining birth rate and a lack of affordable housing in Boise. While Idaho’s population is growing, fewer residents are having children. Between 2005 and 2024, the birth rate among women ages 15-44 decreased from 78.9 per 1,000 to 58.6 per 1,000, according to the National Center for Health Statistics . The slowing birth rate means fewer students entering school, and that’s been a trend across Idaho’s public schools in recent years. Between the 2021-22 and 2025-26 school years, kindergarten enrollment statewide dipped 8.5% while 12th-grade enrollment increased 9.9%. In Boise, both elementary and secondary enrollments have decreased. But younger grades have decreased at a faster rate. This fall, Boise lost 428 elementary students compared to 271 secondary students. “Anytime your seniors are outpacing your incoming kindergarten class annually, which ours have been doing … you have a gap in enrollment,” Hutchison said. There are also students who were previously enrolled in the Boise School District but left for various reasons. Exit data shows that among the students who left the district during the 2024-25 school year: 57% transferred to another public school district or public charter school 17% moved to another state 8% transferred to a homeschool setting 7% transferred to a private school. Boise trustee Alejandro Necochea on Monday asked district administrators to share with the school board more information on the students who leave midyear. “How many kids are still in our community who just dropped out of our radar?” he said. Idaho Education News previously reported that the district cut funding for 17 jobs in anticipation of the enrollment decline. Assistant Superintendent Nick Smith said Monday that district administrators will continue to watch enrollment numbers before Nov. 1 — the cutoff for fall average daily attendance, which determines state funding for employee salaries and benefits. “We do anticipate that (enrollment) will fluctuate between now and Nov. 1,” Smith said, “so we do believe that 600 number that we budgeted on is going to be pretty realistic.”

If a woman incarcerated at the South Idaho Correctional Institution in Kuna has a dentist appointment, she has to walk through the men’s side of the prison to attend it. To do that, correctional staff must shut down much of the men’s side, restricting everybody’s movement to get her to her appointment. There are nearly 400 women and 300 men at the medium-security prison , which was originally designed for men. South Idaho Correctional Institution Warden Jennifer Tyvand (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) South Idaho Correctional Institution Warden Jennifer Tyvand is hoping a new women’s facility, slated to open in December 2027, will help solve many of the challenges of trying to house both men and women there. The new women’s prison is one of three new facilities the Idaho Department of Correction, or IDOC, plans to open within the next year. According to a preliminary budget request, the state agency will ask Idaho legislators in January for around $45.3 million to furnish and operate those new facilities to address a statewide shortage of prison beds. The new facilities will add nearly 1,000 new beds in the state prison system. The Legislature approved funding to build the facilities, but those appropriations didn’t include funding to furnish, equip and staff each of them. In 2022, lawmakers approved $112.4 million for a new women’s prison and $37.6 million for improvements to the medical annex at the Idaho State Correctional Institution in Kuna through House Bill 791. In 2024, the Legislature appropriated $10 million for the new facility in Orofino in HB 768. Bree Derrick (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Correction) “If we don’t open them, first of all, as a state we’d have nearly $200 million of investment that’s going to sit empty,” IDOC Director Bree Derrick said at an interview at the South Idaho Correctional Institution. “… In terms of the management of the population, we would continue to essentially limp along in the same way we have done, which means probably over-reliance on county jails and on out-of-state contract beds. And then, as it relates to the women, the women will remain here for the foreseeable future.” The state is short about 200 beds for women inmates, which means some are sent to county jails, according to the agency budget request. Idaho’s entire prison population is about 10,000 inmates, according to state data , but the total prison capacity sits at just over 8,200. items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) As the Idaho Legislature continues to study the state’s health insurance system before reconvening for the 2027 legislative session, the state’s top insurance official recommended having prolonged study of healthcare issues. The suggestion came soon after Dean Cameron, the director of the Idaho Department of Insurance, started speaking to the Legislature’s Health Insurers Working Group . Idaho Department of Insurance Director Dean Cameron, right. (Photo courtesy of Idaho Department of Insurance) Back when he served in the Legislature — where he served for 25 years — he said that lawmakers had a task force that met throughout the summer studying healthcare issues faced by consumers, businesses and Idahoans. “It might be time to consider dusting that process off,” Cameron said. Then he delved into how the agency regulates health insurers and other insurance companies — and provided a glimpse into some of the common reasons behind complaints, which Cameron urged providers to lodge with his office if they have an issue. “We take our responsibility very seriously,” Cameron said. A significant amount of complaints that the state agency receives against health insurers are related to claims being denied, along with pharmacy benefits and plan cancelations, according to statistics the Department of Insurance shared with the committee. If Idaho insurer met hospital’s pay raise, state employees’ costs would rise, official says According to the state agency’s data, Regence BlueShield of Idaho saw an uptick in complaints that were ultimately resolved by an arbiter — formally called an external reviewer — starting in 2024, soon after the company took over the state’s contract to provide health insurance for state employees and their family members. Cameron told lawmakers that the rise was partly because the company had recently taken over the state contract, and partly because the state had banned covering prescription medication for weight loss in late 2025. Just under a third of the decisions in the 217 complaints Regence faced in 2025 were overturned by external reviewers, according to the Department of Insurance. The state legislative working group was founded after contract negotiations between Portneuf Medical Center in Pocatello and Regence fell through, leading to the hospital to be out of network for the state’s insurer. Last month, the two struck a deal to go back in-network. For the first time, the hospital’s CEO, Nate Carter, addressed the committee Tuesday. Part of the reason this committee was formed, he said, was to navigate through contracting issues — which he said his hospital was glad to have resolved with Regence. “But also this committee is meant for a much larger purpose, which is to assist providers and insurers both in working together to make sure that patients, my neighbors, my friends, and my family have access to high quality care in their respective communities,” Carter said. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. items.body: A quarterly report and an independent audit tell conflicting stories about the Idaho School Benefit Trust’s finances, according to public documents shared by the Idaho Department of Insurance last week. Meanwhile, included in those documents, internal board minutes show the trust painted a rosy picture of low rates and stability and unveil that the trust paid out $1.9 million on a single claim, shedding light on why some claims exceeded expectations this past year. The department is investigating what led to the trust’s collapse and has petitioned the court to take over and rehabilitate the self-funded health care plan that pays medical claims for thousands of public school employees and dependents. As of Tuesday, Fourth District Court Judge Lynn Norton has not yet approved the department’s request. “We understand that districts and other interested parties want answers now, and we ask for the opportunity to complete the examination and its determinations before drawing conclusions,” department spokesperson Julie Robinson wrote in a Monday email to EdNews. After receiving multiple records requests, the department last week posted 11 documents totaling 152 pages on its web page dedicated to sharing information about the trust. The documents include: Independent audits for fiscal years 2024 and 2025 One quarterly report the trust filed last year Three years of the trust’s internal board meeting minutes The department’s two civil filings submitted last month As a self-funded plan, the trust is required to submit unaudited quarterly statements and an annual audit to the department. The state then checks these documents to make sure the trust is complying with statute, including a requirement to keep a certain level of money saved up in surplus. Without enough money in the fund balance, the department has the authority to terminate a plan’s registration. The trust’s unaudited report for the quarter ending on May 31, 2025, shows it had plenty of money in reserves. It needed a minimum of $8.2 million in surplus and had $13.5 million, an excess of $5.3 million. After two years of losses totaling $7.3 million, the trust appeared to be having a good year. The report showed a net gain of $2.4 million for the first nine months of the 2024-25 benefit year, which began Sept. 1, 2024, and ended Aug. 31, 2025. Trustee and treasurer Darren Uranga, also CFO for Elevate Academy, signed the report on Aug. 5. items.title: We can’t stop Idaho from growing, but with more housing options, we can choose how
items.summary: In recent years, eviction and homelessness doubled as regional housing costs climbed roughly 40%, and the gap between wages and home prices keeps widening, writes guest columnist Ali Rabe. (Photo by Getty Images) Every week, public hearings across the Treasure Valley and beyond fill up with an emerging voice: residents, many of whom moved here in the last five to ten years, showing up to vote down
items.body: In recent years, eviction and homelessness doubled as regional housing costs climbed roughly 40%, and the gap between wages and home prices keeps widening, writes guest columnist Ali Rabe. (Photo by Getty Images) Every week, public hearings across the Treasure Valley and beyond fill up with an emerging voice: residents, many of whom moved here in the last five to ten years, showing up to vote down housing options their communities need. They organize, vote, and pressure local officials to reject more housing. I understand where that instinct comes from. I just don’t think it’s pointing us toward the right answer. Idaho leads the nation in housing growth. The data shows it’s still not enough. I grew up in Middleton, surrounded by farm fields. Those fields are gone now, replaced by one-acre lots with little infrastructure to support them. I’ve watched Idaho change in ways that make me sad, and I understand the anti-growth mindset. Too often growth here has meant sprawl, distant subdivisions, and longer commutes. But growth itself isn’t the enemy. Communities grow and change, and that change can make a place better, not worse. The Treasure Valley will keep growing. The question is how. During my nearly seven years leading Jesse Tree , the Treasure Valley’s eviction prevention nonprofit, I watched more and more Idahoans lose their footing here. People who worked full time couldn’t make rent, families were evicted, and some ended up homeless. In recent years, eviction and homelessness doubled as regional housing costs climbed roughly 40%, and the gap between wages and home prices keeps widening. Meanwhile, most of what gets built on our fringe is the same product: large-lot homes pushing half a million dollars, aimed at out-of-state buyers. Young Idahoans, our workforce, and longtime locals are left out. There’s a better path, and it isn’t new. It’s called missing middle housing, and it’s a return to how Idaho used to build. Missing middle housing means duplexes, triplexes, fourplexes, cottage courts, and small-lot homes woven into existing neighborhoods rather than dropped onto the fringe. It’s gentle, incremental density that adds homes without ruining a neighborhood’s character. Look at Idaho’s historic neighborhoods and you’ll find these home types everywhere. This is how our cities grew before exclusionary zoning took hold in the 1970s and made large-lot sprawl the only easy path for developers. It’s also better economics, for residents and for cities. Land is the single largest cost on a developer’s pro forma. When zoning only allows large-lot product, that cost gets baked into every home, which is why half-million-dollar houses keep getting built. Smaller homes on smaller lots bring that cost down and open the door to starter homes again. For cities, more homes per acre means more property value per acre without miles of new pipes, roads, and schools. It’s a better deal for taxpayers on both ends. None of this requires upending the neighborhoods people love. In my experience, when people see what missing middle housing actually is, rather than what they assume it is, most come around. Even hearing opponents soften once they realize it isn’t a five-story apartment complex next door. It’s a duplex that looks like the house beside it. I don’t fault anyone for wanting to protect what they love about this place. I love it too, farm fields and all. But protecting Idaho doesn’t mean freezing it in place, and it certainly doesn’t mean a housing market that only works for people who aren’t from here. It means asking a better question: how do we grow in a way that gives our young people, our workforce, and our own neighbors a shot at homeownership? Missing middle housing is one of the clearest answers we have. If you want to help make the case in your community, Gem State Housing Alliance is activating pro-housing voices across the state, and we’d love to welcome you. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

items.body: OpenAI is partnering with the Boise School District to give educators upgraded access to AI chatbot ChatGPT. The district plans to roll out “ChatGPT Edu” for its teachers in the spring semester. Boise joins more than 100 districts, charters and other K-12 organizations nationwide that have partnered with the company, according to OpenAI. The agreement gives Boise teachers and administrators upgraded access to ChatGPT while tightening data privacy protections. In an August interview with Idaho EdNews, Boise Chief Technology Officer Ryan Gravette called the arrangement “one of the strongest data privacy agreements” he has seen from a partner. Earlier this year, lawmakers had concerns about data privacy when they passed Senate Bill 1227 , which instructs the Idaho Department of Education to develop a statewide framework for integrating generative AI into classrooms. Some teachers already use ChatGPT, which harvests data from user interactions if they use the free version. Gravette — who previously worked at the Idaho Digital Learning Alliance, where he helped set up the same partnership — said he approached OpenAI to bring Boise into the program. He said teachers can use AI to reduce the time they spend doing clerical duties so they can focus on teaching students. “Wh at I think is important is that we’re taking a data-based approach around what really is the data showing,” Gravette said. “And let that guide the direction that the district is taking,” rather than the “emotional direction” of some community members. OpenAI sees an opportunity in schools Partnering with a massive tech company isn’t a first for Boise, Gravette said, adding that the district has agreements with Google, Microsoft and Apple. The OpenAI agreement involves no exchange of money, he said, though Boise purchased $5,000 in ChatGPT credits to allow users to exceed usage limits. Boise Human Resources Director Will Goodman, who formerly filled Gravette’s role, said OpenAI’s push to work with school districts reminds him of similar initiatives by Microsoft and Apple to get their software or hardware into schools at steep discounts. “T heir model was, ‘I f everybody grows up using an Apple product, they will buy an Apple product when they’re an adult,'” Goodman said. Microsoft eventually became the dominant software provider in schools, showing how deeply those early technology choices can shape the market. Gravette theorized OpenAI aims to become a leader in the education sector of tech, a space where Google has long been dominant. items.body: The Boise School District will pay $34,000 to a former student who twice encountered a transgender classmate in the girls’ bathroom last year. The district agreed to a settlement with Jane Doe — a pseudonym — after she filed a lawsuit arguing that the district violated Senate Bill 1100 . The law requires public school students to use bathrooms aligned with their birth sex, and it created a “private cause of action,” which gives students the right to sue a district that doesn’t comply with the law. Last year, the Boise district allowed transgender students to use their preferred bathrooms while SB 1100 was mired in court. After Doe twice encountered a transgender student in the girls’ bathroom at Boise High School, she filed a lawsuit seeking $5,000 for each incident. She also sought additional monetary damages along with attorney fees. The Idaho Family Policy Center (IFPC), a Christian, conservative lobbying group with a legal team that represented Doe, announced Tuesday that the district agreed to pay her $10,000 for the two bathroom encounters along with $24,000 in attorney fees. The settlement closes the first lawsuit brought under SB 1100. IFPC co-authored the bill. Republican state lawmakers enacted it in 2023. “The IFPC Legal Center is honored to secure a settlement for Jane Doe in this groundbreaking case,” IFPC Legal Center Director Caleb Pirc said in a news release. “Other Idaho public schools should take note that compliance with the law isn’t optional.” John Doe — a pseudonym for Jane Doe’s father — said in the news release that his daughter endured a “breach of her privacy.” “Not once but twice she encountered a male student in the female bathroom,” John Doe said in the release. “When she reported the incidents to school staff, she was told that it was their policy to allow males who identify as female to use the bathroom of their choice.” Attorneys for the Boise School District had asked an Ada County judge to dismiss Jane Doe’s lawsuit, arguing that SB 1100 was paused at the time of the bathroom encounters. In a separate case that wrapped up this year , the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals had issued a stay on SB 1100, pausing enforcement of the law between Oct. 26, 2023, and March 20, 2025. Doe encountered a transgender classmate in the girls’ bathroom in January and February of 2025. But Ada County District Judge Lynn Norton denied the district’s motion to dismiss the case. In July, Norton ordered that while the federal stay barred “enforcement” of SB 1100, it didn’t preclude Doe’s private cause of action. Norton allowed the case to proceed. It was scheduled for trial next year before the two parties agreed to a settlement. Dan Hollar, public affairs administrator for the Boise district, said Tuesday that the settlement “resolves disputed claims,” but the district “continues to maintain that it acted appropriately.” “Neither the District nor any of its employees admits, acknowledges, or concedes any fault, wrongdoing, liability, or other misconduct,” Hollar said by email. The specific terms of the settlement “are confidential and will not be disclosed or publicized,” Hollar added. “Out of respect for the privacy of the minor children involved, the District will have no further comment on this matter.”

items.body: An Alaska Airlines jet lands at Newark Liberty International Airport. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor) One of my earliest memories is sitting behind my dad in his airplane, pressing my face to the window, watching the big buildings shrink to look like Lego sets. I remember thinking: I want to fly a plane one day. The memories of flying with my dad – a fixed wing and helicopter pilot who repaired power lines – stayed with me for years of raising three wonderful children and working in sales. It wasn’t until my early 40s that I completed my private pilot license, the first step in my pilot career. I’m currently completing my instrument rating while working toward my commercial certificate, both needed to achieve my long-term goal of building a career in corporate aviation. My story matters now because women don’t need to wait until mid-life to become pilots. If the calling comes in childhood, follow it. Girls in Aviation Day returns to Boise on Saturday, Sept. 19, and I want as many people as possible, especially girls who may assume a cockpit isn’t for them, to see what’s possible. Women hold only about 5.5% to 6% of U.S. airline pilot jobs. This number has barely moved in decades, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Meanwhile, North American airlines expect to be 30,000 pilots short of what they need by 2032, despite the U.S. government projecting that there will be roughly 18,000 new airline and commercial pilot openings this decade. My timeline was unusual and now I’m training while balancing significant family responsibilities that don’t pause for flight lessons. Training is expensive, and self-funding my dream has meant real sacrifice for myself and my family. I’ve asked myself more than once whether it made sense to keep going. My answer has stayed the same: yes. I credit that to the mentorship I’ve received from other women in aviation. A scholarship through Women in Corporate Aviation last year helped me pass my instrument written exam and keep training toward my checkride. I pay it forward by mentoring girls through our local chapter of Women in Aviation and volunteering with events like Girls in Aviation Day, because I wouldn’t be here without seeing the many women before me who have made it to the rank of captain. Girls in Aviation Day brings around 250 girls ages 8 to 18 to Western Aircraft in Boise for a free day of aircraft tours, hands-on activities, and one-on-one time with women working across aviation and aerospace: pilots, engineers, mechanics, dispatchers, air traffic controllers. For many of these girls, it may be the first time they see someone who looks like them doing this job. Representation changes what a kid believes is possible for herself. While I didn’t have many women pilots to point to when I was younger, those in my life are instrumental in keeping me on my career path. I want the girls in the Treasure Valley community to have that now, not decades later. I want women considering aviation later in life, like I did, to know their timeline doesn’t have to look a certain way. Please bring the girls in your life to Western Aircraft at the Boise Airport between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. Registration is free at bit.ly/GIAD2026 . items.body: Idaho State Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield, a Republican running for another term in November, speaks to an attendee after a candidate forum on Aug. 4, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Sean Dolan/EdNews) This story was originally posted on IdahoEdNews.org on Sept. 10, 2026. Debbie Critchfield wants $20 million to help school districts and charters keep pace with inflation, and support at-risk students. Even if the 2027 Legislature signs on, the $20 million would get carved up quickly. But the state superintendent said she prefers to enter the next session with a workable request, and not one that is immediately dismissed as “ridiculous.” “I’d rather ask for something that I believe we can get to,” Critchfield said Wednesday. After budget cuts, Idaho plans to maintain low government spending, state official says In an EdNews interview, Critchfield discussed the 2027-28 spending request she submitted a week ago — and the political calculus that went into her budget. All told, Critchfield is seeking more than $3.3 billion for K-12, a 3.9% increase. But her one new budget request is a $20 million slice of the pie. She wants this increase to go into “operational” spending — commonly called discretionary funds, because districts and charters can use this line item for any purpose. And that makes it a popular request in the K-12 community, Critchfield said Wednesday. So far, she said, she has heard only positive feedback from school administrators. “(It’s) the most flexible and customizable part of the budget for districts and charters.” However, there also would be a lot of pressure on the $20 million. Operational funding, now at $366 million, has essentially been frozen for three years. An increase could help address inflation. Schools could also use the increase to cover unexpected bills from the Idaho School Benefit Trust. Districts and charters are on the hook for much of the trust’s $13 million shortfall — and as EdNews reported this week, employee medical claims could be denied if a member of the trust refuses to pay their share of the $13 million. The trust shortfall came to light in July, but Critchfield’s budget has no money to address it directly. Lastly, the new operational money could support a rewrite of Idaho’s aging school funding formula. Idaho politicians have long discussed changes to the formula, adopted in 1994. Supporters of a rewrite, including Critchfield, want to provide extra funding to support at-risk students, such as special education students. While $20 million won’t cover a new formula entirely, it could provide first-year funding, Critchfield said Wednesday. Dedicated dollars could smooth the transition, covering schools that would lose money under a new formula. And this would be a departure from 2025, when lawmakers debated a funding formula bill that had no dollars attached to it. While Critchfield is pushing the $20 million line item, the Republican is seeking less money for the special education program she navigated through the 2026 Legislature. Her budget contains $1.7 million for a “high-needs” fund, for students who require full-time staff support or costly equipment. This year’s high-needs budget is $5 million. items.body: One by one, Elevate Academy students crossed the stage at Caldwell’s Indian Creek Plaza, each flanked by a first responder or soldier. They stopped at center stage to read the names of Idahoans who died while serving in the military after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks that killed 2,977 people. “United States Army reserve Coby Schwab , 25, Hayden Lake. Never forget.” Then a bell rang. “Army specialist Robert E. Dyas , 21, Nampa. Never forget.” A bell rang again. Quietly, hundreds of students, parents and community members sat and listened. Indian Creek Plaza in Caldwell, decorated for a 9/11 memorial put on by Elevate Academy on Sept. 11, 2026. (Kaeden Lincoln/EdNews) " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/elevate911-4-e1789161229365-1180x692.jpg" class="size-full wp-image-125591" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/elevate911-4.jpg" alt="" width="1920" height="1440" /> Indian Creek Plaza in Caldwell, decorated for a 9/11 memorial put on by Elevate Academy on Sept. 11, 2026. (Kaeden Lincoln/EdNews) “I t’s kind of tough because we go through it, we practice it, and it doesn’t feel as real,” said Sierra Shippy, an Elevate Academy senior and master of ceremonies for the memorial. “ But sitting there and actually hearing the bell ring , it’s just — I don’t know. It’s just so, not disheartening, but in a way it is because those are lives. I t’s just so hard to think about how many people we lost.” After students read the names, former New York policeman Brian Bartley told his story. “A s we were sitting in a class lecture at police academy, my classmates and I heard the roar of a jet engine fly overhead,” Bartley recounted. “This was unusual as Manhattan is a no-fly zone.” He and his fellow rookies found it odd, but thought little of it. They didn’t know the plane was bound for the World Trade Center. Fifteen minutes later, Bartley said, a lieutenant walked into the classroom and told them what happened. Not yet a sworn officer, he would spend the next several days directing traffic and working security around the perimeter of the World Trade Center’s rubble. Bartley went on to serve 20 years in the NYPD. He now drives a school bus in Caldwell for Brown Bus Company. He never spoke publicly about his experience until around five years ago, when he started speaking at Elevate Academy’s 9/11 memorial. “It’s therapeutic,” he said. “ It definitely helps, and it’s more important that it helps remind people about what we’ve lost, what we went through, and teach the next generation so that they know why it’s important, why it’s not just a date on the calendar.” Here are some photos of Friday’s event: Click to view slideshow.

items.body: Wildfire smoke rolls over the skies near Warm Springs along U.S. Highway 26 on July 25, 2026. (Photo by Oregon Department of Transportation) Oregon lawmakers approved nearly $123 million to help cover the costs of this year’s wildfire season, sending money to two state agencies responsible for fighting wildfires. The Oregon Legislature’s Joint Emergency Board agreed to allocate $108 million to the Oregon Department of Forestry and $15 million to the Department of the State Fire Marshal at a morning meeting Thursday. The 20-member board has the authority to allocate funding when the full Legislature isn’t in session. As of late August, wildfires had scorched across 2.5 million acres and cost the state $236.2 million. Those costs are expected to reach $350 million by the end of the wildfire season — putting 2026 on track to surpass the state’s previous $318 million record when wildfires scorched 1.9 million acres in 2024. The forestry department has been able to pay for nearly $79 million of those costs with federal recovery funding, grants and other contributions. With the emergency board’s approval Thursday, the agency will also borrow $150 million from the Oregon State Treasury through three loans over the next three months to maintain solvency through the end of the year. The State Fire Marshal responded to 12 destructive wildfires this year that cost more than $50 million. The agency’s $15 million request will cover funding gaps needed to address those costs. The federal government is expected to reimburse Oregon for some of these costs, though that money can take years to arrive. The Federal Emergency Management Agency still owes Oregon about $92 million in fire management and public assistance grants from 2020. These are grants a state requests if they are facing a catastrophic emergency, and the federal government agrees to pay 75% of the costs. Typically they take about two to three years to be fully released to the states. This is not an unusual amount of money owed, nor is it unusual that it’s taking so long to be reimbursed, according to Joy Krawczyk, a spokesperson for the Oregon Department of Forestry. The slow pace of federal reimbursements frustrated lawmakers. “Through the course of today’s allocations, we’re going to be taking general fund dollars away from our schools, from healthcare, from housing, from public safety, while we’re waiting for reimbursement from the federal government,” said Rep. David Gomberg, D-Otis. Lawmakers on the emergency board thanked all the agencies who worked to put out the wildfires this summer. “It was predicted to be tough,” said Rep. Mark Owens, R-Crane. “We exceeded tough by many levels in that period of time. Without the coordination, the dedication of the state agencies, and I’ll say our Bureau of Land Management, the U.S. Forest Service, Rangeland Fire Protection Associations, rural fire districts and the volunteers that are out there, there’d have been towns and houses taken out.” Oregon Capital Chronicle senior reporter Alex Baumhardt contributed to this story. items.body: Before I was a legislator, I was, and still am, an Idaho mom. Like many parents, I want my children to have the opportunity to receive a good education, find meaningful work and, if they choose, build their lives here in Idaho. That is one reason I believe the conversation surrounding the proposed Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus should include education. America’s demand for reliable electricity is growing rapidly. Data centers, artificial intelligence, and advanced manufacturing are increasing that demand, and advanced nuclear energy could play an important role in meeting it. The Department of Energy recently selected Idaho as one of five states to explore hosting an NLIC. These campuses could include fuel fabrication, enrichment, used-fuel recycling and reprocessing, advanced reactors, power generation, and advanced manufacturing. DOE estimates a campus could attract up to $50 billion in private investment and create nearly 25,000 jobs. Those numbers should get the attention of everyone involved in Idaho education. If Idaho pursues this opportunity, we should also ask: How do we make sure Idaho students are prepared to fill those jobs? Not every career in nuclear energy requires a degree in nuclear engineering. An expanding industry needs engineers and scientists, but it also needs electricians, welders, technicians, mechanics, construction workers, cybersecurity professionals, project managers, and many other skilled employees. We already have pieces of that pipeline throughout Idaho. INL partners with Idaho universities, supports STEM education and internships, and helped establish Idaho State University’s Energy Systems Technology and Education Center. The Center for Advanced Energy Studies brings together INL, Idaho State University, University of Idaho, and Boise State University. College of Eastern Idaho also has partnerships creating pathways into energy careers. We should build on those efforts. That means exposing students to STEM and skilled-trade careers earlier, strengthening CTE and apprenticeship opportunities, and ensuring our community colleges and universities are aligned with the workforce Idaho will need. It also means helping students understand nuclear energy based on science and facts so they can make informed decisions about whether these careers are right for them. INL already projects more than 2,800 hires through fiscal year 2029, even before considering what an NLIC could add. For more than 70 years, Idaho has helped pioneer American nuclear technology. Our experience has taught us about innovation, but also about environmental stewardship, safeguards, and accountability. Those lessons are an asset as we consider what comes next. I want Idaho students to be able to graduate from an Idaho high school, learn a trade or earn a degree here, and then find a good-paying career without having to leave our state. Economic development and education policy cannot operate in separate lanes. If Idaho wants to lead the next generation of nuclear energy, we should prepare the next generation of Idahoans to lead it. That may be one of the greatest opportunities NLIC offers our state. Rep. Erin Bingham represents District 32B in the Idaho House of Representatives, serving Bonneville County. She serves on the House State Affairs, Commerce & Human Resources, and Environment, Energy & Technology committees.

items.body: Hemlock trees in the woods that are part of the Flight 93 crash site. They were marked with spray-paint by searchers in the days and weeks after the crash. This photo is from sometime in 2006. (Photo courtesy of Tim Lambert) The parking lot was dotted with just a handful of cars on this comfortable August morning. It was the first week of school for many families, so visitors were a bit more sparse than usual. After a two-hour drive from Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, to this secluded spot in Somerset County, it was nice to stretch my legs and feel the sun on my face. I had nearly forgotten how windy it can be out here. My brain sort of went on autopilot as my body started to slowly move forward, past the education center and a small group of tourists milling around, and onto a black granite walkway. Every few steps, I’d glance at an engraving in the pathway — marking the time and location of a terrible event that preceded what I’d see when the walkway simply ends. Passing through two towering concrete walls, my eyes were focused on the overlook ahead. The expanse of fields of tall grasses, trees and flowers disappeared from view. I reached the end and stood in front of a waist-high glass window, marked with the phrase: “A common field one day. A field of honor forever.” I was back at the Flight 93 National Memorial. Instinctively, I glanced up at the blue sky. “It would have passed right over my head,” I thought as I looked out at the green field. A boulder marked the approximate area where United Flight 93 met the earth at more than 560 mph on Sept. 11, 2001. Forty innocent passengers and crew as well as four al-Qaida terrorists lost their lives there. It was peaceful now. The sound of birds, crickets and cicadas merged as the wind picked up again. The grass had recently been mowed, and 60-foot-tall hemlock trees still stood around the area that’s come to be known as the “bowl.” Has it really been 25 years since that horrible day? The crash of United Flight 93 is marked by a boulder at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Stonycreek Township, Somerset County, on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Tim Lambert/Pennsylvania Capital-Star) The rebellion Perhaps the story of Flight 93 has faded over the last quarter century, so it might be a good time to pause for a refresher. The cross-country flight was headed from Newark, New Jersey, to San Francisco when it was delayed on the runway for about 25 crucial minutes. Takeoff occurred about four minutes before the first jetliner struck the World Trade Center in New York. Once in the sky, the four al-Qaida terrorists took control of the plane somewhere over northeast Ohio. Because of the late takeoff, passengers and crew members were able to gather invaluable information through 37 phone calls to loved ones about the attacks in New York and at the Pentagon outside of Washington, D.C., and what was likely their fate too. So, they came together to try to retake the hijacked jetliner and protect innocent people on the ground. Investigators believe the intended target was the U.S. Capitol, but when faced with the uprising, the terrorists chose to bring the plane down amid the struggle for control of the cockpit. After strikes on the symbols of America’s financial and military strength, al-Qaida designed the fourth blow to destroy the very seat of democracy. Thanks to the actions of 40 people who found courage amid the most terrifying experience of their lives, the terrorists failed in the final act of their attack. (Photo courtesy of the University of Idaho) This story was originally posted on IdahoEdNews.org on Sept. 9, 2026. University of Idaho President C. Scott Green will retire on June 30. Green made the announcement during the president’s “state of the university” address Wednesday — an annual event that took a sudden and emotional turn. Addressing the campus community at his alma mater, Green recounted success stories from his seven-year tenure, including advances in enrollment, research and athletics. He also reflected on the challenges of leading the U of I through a global pandemic and in the aftermath of the November 2022 off-campus murders of four students. Flowers and candles left for a makeshift memorial sit near police tape at the site of a quadruple murder of four University of Idaho students on Jan. 3, 2023, in Moscow, Idaho. items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho state government agencies’ budget requests for the next fiscal year are now publicly available. The requests, which are online on the Division of Financial Management’s website , are for Idaho’s fiscal year 2028, which starts July 1, 2027. After ‘tight budget year,’ Idaho ends fiscal year with positive cash balance On the heels of a 2026 Idaho legislative session marked by budget cuts after years of state tax cuts, the requests outline the state’s strategy of continuing to operate state agencies and public programs with less funding, according to the governor’s budget chief, Lori Wolff. In a media briefing last week, Wolff told reporters that non-discretionary funding for Medicaid, state prisons and public schools is eating up most of a recent projection of increased revenue. “We were very tight on our bottom line before, so it doesn’t give us a whole lot of room,” Wolff told reporters. “That really quickly takes up most of the increase in our revenue,” she said. “So, our focus this year is going to be on keeping those budgets at where we set them last year.” In May, she wrote a memo to state agencies instructing them to only submit barebones budgets, and that the next budget year was not the time to start restoring budget cuts . The budget request for the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare — the state’s largest government agency that runs Medicaid and other public assistance programs — is the only budget plan that hasn’t been published yet, the governor’s spokesperson, Emily Callihan, said in a statement. She said officials expect to post the agency’s budget request Tuesday. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The requests are one of the first major steps in the process to fund state government. In January, Idaho Gov. Brad Little typically releases his own proposed state budget. Then the Idaho Legislature, which meets during the first few months of the calendar year, considers budget requests by state agencies and the governor as lawmakers draft budget bills. In recent years, Idaho’s powerful budget-setting committee, the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee, has shifted to a different budgeting process that splits agency budgets into barebones funding and new spending. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho National Laboratory) One of the most critical issues facing Idaho is one that has received little attention but has profound consequences for the future of our state – the agreement that would make Idaho the dumping ground for a third of the radioactive waste generated in our country. It’s not surprising that Idahoans don’t know much about this issue. Gov. Brad Little, who is pursuing this agreement , and U.S. Sen. Jim Risch have said precious little or nothing about it, apparently wanting to keep it under the radar until they are safely re-elected in November. New nuclear campus deal would require Idaho to accept, store spent nuclear fuel, radioactive waste Congressman Mike Simpson applauded the agreement , saying it will bring jobs to his eastern Idaho district. “Idaho didn’t become the nation’s nuclear leader by being afraid of hard problems. It became the leader by being the state willing to do the difficult, careful work that others wouldn’t. That’s still the right instinct now,” he wrote. The Trump administration will choose three states to create what it calls a “Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus.” The other states in the running for this dubious honor besides Idaho are Utah, Tennessee, Louisiana and Oklahoma. The chosen states will each have to receive 33 percent of the radioactive waste generated by the other 47 states. The public did not know that Gov. Little agreed to be one of the states until the Department of Energy announced it in late July. The memorandum of understanding that Little signed in July without informing Idahoans said: “The host agreement shall provide for the acceptance of out-of-state used nuclear fuel, spent fuel, and high-level radioactive waste.” In its announcement, the Trump administration promised that the campus will boost manufacturing, create jobs, promote American energy independence, and attract other unnamed financial investments. Of course, we don’t know what this means since Little and our congressional delegation have not told us what’s in the fine print. Idaho’s long history with nuclear waste To put the importance of this issue in perspective, it is important to understand Idaho’s long and dark history with radioactive waste. Starting in the 1940s, the federal energy site in eastern Idaho, which is now called the Idaho National Laboratory, became the repository for much of the nation’s nuclear radioactive waste. The issue came to a head in the late 1970s when the press reported that the federal facility had regularly poured low-level radioactive liquid waste down an injection well above the Snake River Aquifer, which is the size of Lake Erie and provides much of the water for southern Idaho’s farmers and ranchers. There was also concern about other radioactive liquid waste being stored in containers buried above the aquifer. I covered energy issues for t he Idaho Statesman at the time and reported on the controversy over this waste. There was concern among Idaho’s political leaders because the federal site was also known for its porous volcanic soil and seismic activity. Coverage of the issue made front page news for months. That same year the General Accounting Office recommended that Idaho become a permanent repository for the nation’s radioactive waste. That proposal came nine years after the federal government promised to remove the existing waste from Idaho. The GAO report was quickly opposed by then Gov. John Evans and even a Republican legislator from Boise who introduced a bill in the Legislature to ban any shipment of radioactive waste into our state.
