items.body: Most of the Kuna district’s schools are below capacity, some by hundreds. That’s despite Kuna’s rapid population growth, leaving the district with a disconnect between community growth and public school enrollment. Superintendent Marcus Myers laid out the district’s capacity and enrollment numbers in a presentation to trustees Tuesday night. Hubbard Elementary: 263 students in a building with a capacity of 400. Indian Creek Elementary: 238 students in a building with a capacity of 375. Fremont Middle School: 532 students in a building with a capacity of 750. Kuna Middle School: 726 students in a building with a capacity of 960. Enrollment has dropped by nearly 4% in the district since last school year, falling from 5,703 to 5,501. Yet in 2025, the U.S. Census Bureau named Kuna one of the fastest-growing cities in the nation. “Right now we do have some room, and we want our classrooms full for the sake of our kids and for the great opportunities that we afford to kids,” Myers told trustees. Some students are choosing alternatives to traditional public schools. About 2% of school-aged children within the district’s boundaries attend charters schools, Myers told Idaho Education News. Increasingly, parents have more options beyond traditional public schools. Valor Classical Academy, a charter school, opened its doors this year with around 450 students enrolled. Myers wants to have conversations with local families choosing charters to understand what influenced their decision. “It could have nothing to do with the Kuna School District,” he said. Myers told trustees he’s also working with the city to identify demographics of families moving into the area to learn how many have school-age children. He’s unsure when he will have the data. Kuna’s enrollment appears to reflect a statewide trend : Despite continued population growth across the state, overall K-12 enrollment is declining, particularly among elementary-age students. One factor is declining birth rates, which fell from over 16 per 1,000 residents in 2007 to under 12 per 1,000 residents in 2024, according to U.S. census data. Kuna has also seen its heaviest declines among elementary students. Some parents also cited homeschooling in a recent Kuna School District survey. Other families may be choosing private or charter schools, though it’s unclear how many students leaving public schools are taking advantage of Idaho’s $50 million Parental Choice Tax Credit. The Idaho State Tax Commission won’t release data showing how many recipients previously enrolled their children in public schools. items.body: Idaho’s colleges and universities hope to reverse a big budget cut from last year. The schools would use much of the money to bolster high-demand academic fields or cover the cost of growth. The budget request centers on a complicated line item that Gov. Brad Little refused to fund in 2026 — enrollment workload adjustment, or EWA. Using a three-year average of weighted credit hours, EWA is designed to provide additional money to growing colleges and universities. But with enrollment growing throughout the higher ed system, all eight of the state’s colleges and universities would stand to get some EWA funding. The EWA proposal: A breakdown The higher ed budget requests, submitted by the State Board of Education last week , come to more than $884 million. The EWA line item comes to a relatively small fraction, $12.1 million. Here’s where that money would go, and why the colleges and universities are pushing for a share: Boise State University: $5.3 million . Boise State would focus its money on high-demand programs in health professions, engineering and construction management. Some money would go into University Foundations, required undergraduate classes across all disciplines. “This support is vital to reduce student waitlists and faculty overloads, maintain accreditation, expand program capacity, and ensure students have access to required courses and high-quality instruction to ensure timely graduation,” according to Boise State’s request. About $2.2 million would go into personnel, including 18 faculty positions. University of Idaho: $2.6 million . The U of I plans to fund teaching assistant positions and student support through its Strategic Enrollment Management division. College of Western Idaho: $1.3 million . The money would go entirely into personnel, including five staff positions and nine instructors in high-demand fields. “(CWI) estimates that the student population will attempt over 145,000 credit hours in the 2026-27 academic year,” CWI said in its budget request. “This is 21% more than the 119,988 credits attempted in the 2023-2024 academic year, just three years ago.” College of Southern Idaho: $986,000 . CSI would put its request fully into personnel — and pay raises. “The funding of EWA would allow CSI to increase wages across many areas of the college,” the college said in its request. North Idaho College: $577,000 . NIC would put the entire request into personnel. In its request, NIC forecasts a 6% enrollment increase this fall, on the heels of a combined 20% increase over the previous two years. Lewis-Clark State College: $542,000 . All money would go toward personnel. This would include math, science and writing tutors and adjunct funding “to support student success and retention,” the college said in its request. College of Eastern Idaho: $528,000 . The CEI request is not tied to specific jobs, but all the money would go into personnel costs. CEI is expecting a 5% to 10% enrollment increase in 2027-28 — the year of the proposed budget request. Idaho State University: $347,000 . All funding would go into personnel, including “full- and part-time faculty” in healthcare professions and the STEM fields of science, technology, engineering and math. items.body: UPDATED 9/9/2026 with details about how the Assistance League uses its thrift shop revenue. Operation School Bell started in someone’s garage more than 30 years ago. Today, the volunteer program fills a warehouse with boxes of back-to-school supplies and new clothes for needy elementary students in Boise, Kuna and West Ada districts. The massive volunteer program begins with the Assistance League of Boise, which is funded by a small Garden City thrift store that generated $1 million last year, the most it’s ever made. It’s open Wednesday through Saturday for dropping off items or shopping for hand-picked, new-to-you treasures. Eighty percent of the store’s revenue goes toward funding Assistance League philanthropy efforts like Operation School Bell. This year, hundreds of students benefitted. “ I was raised by a single mom, so I would have benefited from these programs as a young student,” said Rebecca Kochvar, who has volunteered with the Assistance League of Boise since 2012. “It definitely feels like a real joy for me to be able to do this for students that would have been me in kindergarten through sixth grade.” Here’s how it works: Counselors and educators select students in need of clothes and supplies during the first days of school. These students are then transported in buses to the Assistance League of Boise’s “store,” a large room resembling the children’s clothing section of a department store, complete with racks of puffer coats, full-length mirrors and changing rooms. After choosing their new clothes, students get fitted for a new pair of shoes in another room. Volunteers — largely retired women — help kids find what fits. items.body: (BOISE) – Last year when I was pressed to identify cuts to our public schools, I declined. I knew schools couldn’t sustain mid-year cuts, let alone ongoing reductions. When I submit a K-12 public school budget, it comes after months of consideration and work, informed by where schools are financially and what they need. In the background of this back-to-school season, my team and I have been preparing that budget. Everything we see at the surface of our schools – buses transporting students, teachers welcoming kids to their classrooms, and students learning and succeeding – is fueled by the dollars allocated through the K-12 public school budget. Preparing it is a huge responsibility, and in this tight fiscal environment, we had to be agile in finding money and allocating it effectively. We have to look at the pot of money available and find the most efficient ways to use it so districts and charters can maximize their appropriation for the betterment of their students and communities. Here are some things I’d like Idahoans to know about this year’s requested K-12 budget: We prepared this budget knowing that the one-time funding the Legislature appropriated to support high-needs students in FY27 was just that: one-time. Amidst cutbacks and reductions, we successfully funded a new policy with interest from existing accounts. That matters. We were very clear that this wasn’t the long-term fix and that we’d return with another request tied to interest. We had to work again this year to secure funding for FY28. That work meant funding for high-needs students was $1.7 million, rather than zero. Our commitment is unchanged, but the current funding mechanism requires us to return to the negotiation table to receive any support for this much-needed fund. That broken mechanism – the reason we’re negotiating one-time funding instead of ongoing support – is one of the most important issues this budget begins to address. During the 2026 legislative session, my department and I had countless conversations about overhauling Idaho’s public school funding formula, created in 1994. Revising that formula to get the right funding into the right places will help solve problems for high-needs students, our educators, and our educational communities. It will create a flow of money that reflects today’s needs, not 1994’s. To say that work will not come with growing pains would be naïve. That’s why we’re asking for $20 million in new operational funding. Operational funding allows schools to address a variety of needs and, most importantly, is the largest source of dollars used to fund special education services. Your child’s classroom should not have to endure these growing pains. This budget request helps ensure it won’t. This request should also assure taxpayers of one thing: we remain committed to supporting students who need more to succeed while moving toward a solution that eliminates the need for one-time asks and constant negotiation. We want a funding formula that works for Idaho’s modern classrooms, and this budget request is an important step in that direction.

(Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star) Across the country, state election officials are waiting to discover if federal courts will allow the Trump administration’s restrictions on mail-in voting to take effect. In Idaho, like many other states , election officials are nervous the changes might come too close to the 2026 midterm elections, which are less than two months away on Nov. 3. Why the rushed Postal Service plan for mail-in voting has states in a panic The changes — proposed in a new U.S. Postal Service rule that implements an executive order by President Donald Trump — would require federal review of the design of absentee ballots and impose new rules on the design of envelopes containing absentee ballots, among other things. “In the moment, the biggest concern … is just we’re so close to the election,” Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, the state’s top election official and an elected Republican, said in an interview last week. “There’s the practical implications of getting absentee ballots out.” McGrane said he isn’t sure that Idaho or other states would be able to fully comply with the USPS rule if it takes effect before this year’s election. He said county clerks across Idaho, who run the state’s elections, are busy finalizing ballots to print and mail out absentee ballots to military and overseas voters by Sept. 19. In Idaho’s largest county, Ada — which is home to Boise — election officials have told the state they need to know about any changes to ballots by Wednesday in order to make changes before they print the ballots, said Trent Tripple, the Republican elected county clerk for Ada County. He said he also worries about making big changes months before the election. “If you want the most secure election possible, do not put artificial timelines and make us change things at the last second,” he said in an interview. “If you’re doing that, I guarantee you there will be mistakes that are made — because we don’t have the time. We can’t back up an election.” And that’s all on top of other potential ballot changes facing Idaho election officials as the Idaho Supreme Court weighs a lawsuit by the organizers of Proposition 1, an abortion legalization ballot initiative, that challenges state officials’ descriptions of the initiative . items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Supreme Court building in Boise as seen on Jan. 14, 2026. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The Idaho Supreme Court on Friday unanimously ruled that state officials must redraft explanations of the effect of voting for or against the proposed abortion rights initiative that will appear on voters’ Nov. 3 general election ballots. The court does not have the authority to write new language, but told the offices of the Idaho Attorney General and Secretary of State that they must submit revised ballot language to the court by 5 p.m. Saturday — around 24 hours after the decision was entered. Idaho Supreme Court Justice Gregory Moeller, right, asks a question during a hearing in this April 25, 2025, file photo. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) The decision, written by Justice Gregory Moeller, found that neither the “yes” or “no” effect statements met the law’s requirements. “A statement is not ‘clear’ if it leaves voters uncertain about a principal legal consequence of their choice, and it does not describe ‘the effect’ of a vote if it materially misstates that consequence,” Moeller wrote. “Conciseness permits Respondents to omit unnecessary detail; it does not permit them to convey an inaccurate picture of the effect of a specific vote.” The ballot “effect statements,” required under state law to be a clear and concise explanation of the impacts of a yes or no vote, were written by Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador and Secretary of State Phil McGrane. The state’s high court heard oral arguments Wednesday and issued a speedy ruling as election officials neared a Sept. 11 deadline to be able to send ballots to military and overseas voters. Supporters of the initiative, called Prop 1, filed a lawsuit on Aug. 27, arguing that the drafted effect statements of “yes” or “no” votes on the ballot measure were “misleading” and “confusing.” Attorneys representing Labrador and McGrane defended the statements in court, arguing they were the clearest and shortest way to inform voters. Joe Parris, a spokesperson for the secretary of state, said Friday the office is working to comply with the order. “We appreciate the Idaho Supreme Court’s prompt review of Proposition One yes-and-no effect statements,” Parris said in an email. “As directed by the court, we are working closely with the Attorney General’s Office to prepare and submit revised statements. (Photo illustration by Getty Images) A panel of judges has placed on hold a federal court order protecting an Idaho fetal medicine doctor from prosecution for abortions performed in specific circu
items.body: Idaho’s abortion ban applies to any stage of pregnancy, with affirmative defenses for cases of rape and incest with an accompanying police report and if an abortion is necessary to save a patient’s life. (Photo illustration by Getty Images) A panel of judges has placed on hold a federal court order protecting an Idaho fetal medicine doctor from prosecution for abortions performed in specific circumstances. The order means Idaho’s abortion laws are fully in effect, with only exemptions to protect the life of the mother, or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester if a police report has been filed. Doctors who perform abortions outside of those exemptions face felony penalties and revocation or suspension of their medical license. Idaho federal judge narrows abortion ruling to only protect Boise doctor who filed lawsuit The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel on Thursday blocked a ruling that would’ve carved out new exemptions in Idaho’s strict abortion ban for the doctor challenging the law. The order will be in place until Ninth Circuit judges are scheduled to hear arguments on Sept. 22. Previously, U.S. District of Idaho Court Judge B. Lynn Winmill wrote in an 81-page decision on Aug. 13 that abortions could be performed in cases where the mother faced serious health risks or risk of self-harm, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. However, after Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador appealed the ruling, Winmill n arrowed the decision to only protect the doctor who filed the lawsuit challenging Idaho’s abortion ban, Dr. Stacy Seyb. Seyb, represented by attorneys from the Lawyering Project and Legal Voice, challenged the constitutionality of Idaho abortion ban’s limited exceptions “The Constitution protects pregnant people’s access to life- and health-preserving abortion care,” Lawyering Project Executive Director Stephanie Toti said in an email to the Sun “We are hopeful that the court of appeals will allow that care to resume after it hears oral argument later this month.” Idaho Family Policy Center attorneys file brief in support of law on half of Idaho lawmakers Attorneys with the Idaho Family Policy Center, a conservative Christian lobbying group, filed a brief in support of Idaho’s abortion ban on behalf of 54 Idaho state legislators. Idaho Family Policy Center Legal Director Caleb Pirc wrote that Winmill’s decision went beyond his authority. “The district court improperly made policy for the people of Idaho,” Pirc wrote. “It may have thought its policy was better than the Legislature’s, but that was not its judgment to make.” The brief says that the authority to create abortion policy rests solely with the Legislature. The lawmakers represented by the brief include 37 House representatives and 17 senators, all Republicans, including leaders from both chambers. items.body: From left, incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, Democrat David Roth, and independent Todd Achilles. Idaho Democrat David Roth, who had been running for the U.S. Senate seat held by Idaho Republican Jim Risch, officially withdrew his name from the ballot just days before the deadline. Roth submitted his withdrawal form on Aug. 28, citing a “lack of support from Democratic Party,” according to the form obtained by the Idaho Capital Sun in a public records request. A spokesperson for the Idaho Democratic Party declined to comment. Roth faced pressure from fellow Democrats to clear way for independent candidate Roth announced he was ending his campaign on July 28, the Idaho Capital Sun reported. He had faced strong pressure from supporters of independent candidate Todd Achilles, who argued an independent had a better chance of defeating the longtime incumbent in a head-to-head race. Roth did not endorse Achilles. Roth told the Sun he didn’t want to drop out, but he felt like he didn’t have a choice. He’d also received a letter from leaders of Ada County Democrats asking him to drop out , the Spokesman-Review reported. “Without support from Ada County, I mean that really hindered fundraising or campaign ability,” Roth told the Sun in a phone interview. “And when you have so many people who hold leadership positions in the party advocating for a candidate besides their nominee, it makes it really just impossible.” Roth’s most recent federal election filing shows he garnered about $14,600 in contributions but that his campaign had about $10,100 in debts and loans to be paid back, as of June 30. Roth ran for federal office in 2022 and 2024 and for the state Legislature in 2020. He said this run was “probably the worst experience I’ve ever been through in my entire life.” “And I’ve been through a lot,” he said. He expressed disappointment in his party leaders for not supporting the Democratic nominee in the race after he won his primary contest in May. “It’s an unfortunate situation,” he said. “I think the Democratic voters of Idaho have really lost their opportunity to have a voice, and I think it just goes to show how broken our whole system is.” Achilles’ most recent campaign finance filing shows he’s raised nearly $700,000, although his campaign has recently advertised he’s collected over $1 million. Risch’s warchest was more than $4.4 million as of June 30. The Federal Election Commission requires quarterly reporting on campaign contributions and expenditures, and the next filing deadline is Oct. 15. Without Roth’s formal withdrawal, his name would’ve still appeared on the Nov. 3 general election ballot. Achilles’ campaign has repeatedly said his odds are better if the contest is between him and Risch. “I respect Roth running and making the decision that the campaign just didn’t have the resources it needed to be competitive,” Achilles said in an interview. “I think it’s all about being competitive.” After Roth’s withdrawal, Achilles said his campaign’s plan is to, “keep doing what we’re doing, which is just being out there talking Idahoans and you know working hard on a campaign.” Risch in an interview for an August story told the Sun he was not concerned after Roth announced his departure from the race. “I know people are getting excited all of a sudden because I was running against two Democrats, and now I’m running against one Democrat,” Risch said, referencing that Achilles previously was a Democratic state legislator. “I’ve done that all my life.” Risch, Achilles, independent Natalie Fleming and Libertarian Matt Loesby will appear on ballots for the U.S. Senate race. The Idaho Department of Correction on Aug. 28 joined the 287(g ) program, which allows local law enforcement to carry out some limited immigration enforcement with supervision from federal authorities, according to ICE records of participating agencies. Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little gives his State of the State Address from the House chambers on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “Idaho has a responsibility to uphold the rule of law and protect the people of our state,” Gov. Brad Little said in a press release. “This agreement gives Idaho another tool to make sure criminal aliens who are subject to federal immigration enforcement are transferred to federal custody when they have completed their Idaho sentences. Idaho will continue working with the Trump administration to secure our communities and support the enforcement of our nation’s laws.” The state prison agency’s agreement follows what’s called the “warrant service” model, which allows designated officers within the agency to serve warrants to undocumented people in custody. The agreement “formalizes a process IDOC has already been using to assist ICE,” according to a press release from the governor’s office. Correction staff have historically provided ICE with information on inmates with felony convictions to allow the federal agents to identify those who may be subject to immigration detainers, which are requests by ICE to hold individuals to prevent the release of people who may be undocumented, the release said. Bree Derrick (Photo from Idaho Department of Correction) “IDOC has a longstanding responsibility to coordinate with our federal partners when individuals in our custody are subject to federal immigration enforcement,” IDOC Director Bree Derrick said in the press release. “This agreement strengthens that coordination and gives our department a clear, formal process for serving ICE warrants and transferring individuals into federal custody when their Idaho sentences are complete.” The state prison agency also “facilitates due process hearings for individuals undergoing deportation proceedings and coordinates with ICE when Idaho sentences are satisfied,” the release said. This agreement was funded by the governor’s office emergency funds. As of May, ISP had transported more than 80 people out of correctional facilities, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. An Idaho Capital Sun analysis found some cases where charges were dismissed or still pending when the person was transported to an ICE facility. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Months after protestors wouldn’t leave the lobby of the Idaho governor’s office in an attempt to meet with him over anti-transgender bills, a jury on Tuesday found a local minister guilty on a misdemeanor trespassing charge. The jury found the Rev. Sara LaWall — who wore a clerical collar under a rainbow speckled blazer as she sat in court — guilty of trespassing after prosecutors said she remained in the governor’s office after being warned it was closed for the night during a protest of anti-trans bills this spring. Idaho’s transgender bathroom ban is now the law. How will police enforce it? That’s still unclear. After the jury delivered the verdict, LaWall, the minister for the Boise Unitarian Universalist Fellowship, told reporters that the possible prison sentence she could face would be less time than judges can dole out for violations of Idaho’s new criminal transgender bathroom ban . “That just feels wholly unfair and outsized and ridiculous,” LaWall told reporters after her trial. “… The jury found me guilty of staying in the governor’s office after being told to leave. I didn’t dispute those facts. But someone going to the bathroom now has a higher sentence, and that just feels so disproportionate and so wrong.” Under state law , her trespassing charge is punishable by up to six months in prison. The state’s bathroom ban allows for up to a year in prison on a first offense and up to five years on repeat offenses. Minutes after the nearly full-day trial finished Tuesday, the jury reached its verdict. LaWall will be sentenced on the charge later. Idaho 4th District Judge Adam Kimball scheduled her sentencing for Sept. 17. LaWall’s attorney requested her sentencing be delayed instead of issued Tuesday evening. She hopes at her sentencing she can share more about why she was at the governor’s office. “I have really mixed feelings,” LaWall said of the verdict. “It’s hard not to feel a little emotional about the verdict, but I don’t — I’m not entirely surprised. I took the stand and said as much as the judge allowed me to say about why we were there, which wasn’t very much, and that was disappointing to me to not be able to tell more of the story about why we were there.” LaWall was one of nine protestors who were arrested on trespassing charges at the April 1 protest. At the protest, LaWall and others waited in the lobby in the governor’s office for more than three hours. The protest came a day after Gov. Brad Little signed into law what advocates call the most extreme criminal transgender bathroom ban in the nation. Protestors were also attempting to meet with him and urge him to veto a bill that requires teachers and doctors to out transgender minors to their parents , or face lawsuits. items.summary: A Flock Automated License Plate Reader near the Lowe's on Overland Road in Boise, as captured on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Valentin Termite/Idaho Capital Sun) Congressman Russ Fulcher, R-Idaho (Photo courtesy of Russ Fulcher’s official website) Idaho Republican U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher signed on to federal legislation to limit federal law enforcement’s access to data from automated license plate reade
items.body: A Flock Automated License Plate Reader near the Lowe's on Overland Road in Boise, as captured on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Valentin Termite/Idaho Capital Sun) Congressman Russ Fulcher, R-Idaho (Photo courtesy of Russ Fulcher’s official website) Idaho Republican U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher signed on to federal legislation to limit federal law enforcement’s access to data from automated license plate readers, like Flock cameras, and other surveillance equipment. Fulcher announced Monday in a press release that he is co-sponsoring H.R. 9716 , called the Protecting Rights in Video and Equipment Acquired Discovery Act, or Privacy Act. The legislation would, in most cases, require federal law enforcement to obtain a warrant from a federal judge before accessing surveillance data from state and local systems, including cameras that capture images of vehicle occupants, long-range microphones, electronic fingerprint detection technology, and “substantially similar technology” as determined by the U.S. attorney general, according to the press release. “I’m proud to sign on to this legislation to protect the privacy rights of Idahoans from increasingly intrusive surveillance data collection and to prohibit the widespread deployment of such surveillance tools with federal dollars,” Fulcher said in the press release. “It’s simple: if the federal government wants to access state and local systems’ data on citizens, they need to get a warrant.” The legislation would also put time limits on the retention of data federal authorities obtained, unless a court authorizes an extension or the data is needed as evidence for ongoing prosecution. The bill would also prohibit federal funds from being used to purchase or install surveillance devices, with some exceptions for systems used solely for toll collections on federally funded highways, school violence prevention programs, grants provided under the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act, and portable systems for specific law enforcement operations with a warrant. The bill, brought by Texas Republican U.S. Rep. Keith Self, was introduced July 15 and has not yet been voted on by a committee. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idahoans have expressed concerns about surveillance cameras A number of Idaho cities statewide have contracts for automated license plate readers, called ALPRs, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. Flock is the most common and well-known brand of this type of camera. In July, nearly 100 residents filled the Caldwell City Council chambers, and about a dozen of them spoke about their concern about the city’s use of Flock cameras , the Idaho Press reported. All eyes on Flock as Idaho navigates surveillance technology across the state A 2025 Idaho state law prevents these readers from being used for anything other than “the investigation of felony, misdemeanor crimes, traffic accidents or to search for missing or endangered persons.” However, Twin Falls cameras were searched at least 631 times in March, May and June of 2026 for immigration-related searches, the Sun reported. The searches originated from outside Idaho, and later the Twin Falls Police Department changed its network sharing policies to avoid inadvertently running afoul of Idaho law and its own restrictions on immigration searches. In March, then-Jerome County Sheriff George Oppedyk used Flock cameras to search for his wife’s vehicle hundreds of times between July and September 2025, KMVT reported. Oppedyk retired in April. In early August, the Washington Post reported that at least 50 law enforcement officers across the nation had been charged with or accused of misusing the cameras to track women. Fulcher’s office regularly polls constituents who email him, and recent polls found that data privacy was one of their top concerns, Fulcher told the Idaho Capital Sun in an Aug. 12 interview. “The data privacy stuff, especially recently with the Flock cameras, that has got a lot of people on edge,” Fulcher said. items.body: A replica of the Liberty Bell sits outside of the Idaho Statehouse, as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) In May 1950, Idaho’s very own version of the Liberty Bell arrived in the Gem State. Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth (Photo courtesy of the Idaho State Treasurer’s Office) Nearly a year later, the bell found its home: Sitting prominently in front of grand steps leading up to the Idaho State Capitol — and being loudly rung by passersby. But before it was mounted at the state’s Capitol, the bell toured the state on the back of a pickup truck. And as Americans commemorate the nation’s 250th birthday this year, Idaho’s Liberty Bell is headed back on tour . “We want to have people experience the birth of a nation,” Idaho Treasurer Julie Ellsworth said in an interview. “… We want a memorable thing that touches every place of Idaho.” The tour starts Wednesday with a round of stops in East Idaho, starting in Pocatello and working its way further east, before visiting each of the state’s 44 counties. But how did Idaho even get its own version of the Liberty Bell? The bell — modeled after the cracked original in Philadelphia that has become a national symbol — was one of many cast and given to states in an effort to sell U.S. savings bonds, according to a history of the bell prepared by the Idaho State Historical Society. Idaho’s replica of the Liberty Bell, moved from its typical home, sits on the back of a Ford F-450 flatbed truck. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho State Treasurer’s Office) GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Trucking a state artifact This will be one of the few instances — outside of its recent restoration — when Idaho’s Liberty Bell has left its home at the Capitol. State officials designed this tour to mimic the original tour of the bell from 76 years ago. On its journey across Idaho, the state’s Liberty Bell will sit on the rear axle of a flatbed Ford F-450 pickup. The state is leasing the custom truck for free from Kendall Ford, an auto dealer in the Boise area, Ellsworth said. The new truck has a few more bells and whistles than the original truck had — like enhanced suspension and Spudjamin Franklin, one of many “Revolutionary Spuds” that the state treasurer created to celebrate America’s 250th anniversary. But it’s also missing something that the original truck, a custom Ford R-5 flatbed, had: a loudspeaker, which was used to promote the sale of U.S. savings bonds, according to Janet Gallimore, the executive director of the Idaho State Historical Society, which cares for the state’s artifacts and helped plan the bell’s recent restoration. The 1950 tour of Idaho’s replica of the Liberty Bell was to promote the sale of U.S. savings bonds. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho State Treasurer’s Office) “I … just love the symbology of the bell and what it means, what it meant for obviously the beginnings of our country and the founding of our country, but what that idea of liberty, justice, self-government means to people today. Because it’s a powerful symbol of those things that make us American,” she said in an interview. On the road, the bell will be encased in a cloth cover. At its stops in each county, it will remain on the bed of the truck for display. When will Idaho’s Liberty Bell be near you? Officials aren’t releasing a daily schedule of where the bell will be in each town at a given time until closer to the dates. But Ellsworth says every child that they see on this tour will get a copy of Spudjamin Franklin’s new graphic novel-styled autobiography, which she wrote. Ellsworth said she’ll try to join the tour as much as she can. “It is so symbolic of everything about liberty,” she said of the bell. “But it’s tangible. It’s touchable. It’s understandable.” On Wednesday, the bell will make its journey from Boise to Pocatello — before beginning a nearly three-week tour across East Idaho.
